title: Trust Is Contagious, or Why Trust Exercises at Offsites Are So Important
author: Admired Leadership
summary: Admired Leadership draws on a review of 21 studies covering more than 11,000 people to make a research-backed case that trust is contagious across a team, not just between the two people directly involved in a trustworthy exchange. A single positive interaction is enough to shift a person's general baseline willingness to trust others — and, symmetrically, a single betrayal makes people more suspicious even of bystanders who had nothing to do with it. The piece argues this dynamic is good news for leaders: because trust experiences snowball, leaders can deliberately manufacture low-stakes situations — offsites, shared-mistake discussions, cooperative challenges — where trust is extended and rewarded, gradually building real evidence behind the belief that 'we are a team that trusts each other.' The article closes by reframing trust-building exercises not as feel-good team activities but as a deliberate leadership tool for shifting a team's overall climate.
points: Cites a review of 21 studies (11,000+ participants) showing a single interaction with a trustworthy person shifts a person's general baseline willingness to trust unrelated others, not just their trust in that one individual.

The effect is symmetric and contagious in both directions: one person's broken promise makes the whole team warier, while one person's follow-through makes the whole team more willing to take risks on each other.
People systematically overestimate both how likely others are to be trustworthy after one good interaction, and how emotionally rewarding extending that trust will feel — a bias leaders can leverage.

Reframes trust-building exercises (offsites, obstacle courses, sharing professional mistakes) as deliberate engineering of low-stakes situations where trust can be extended and rewarded, rather than as filler team-building activities.

The specific activity matters less than the structure: team members extend trust, others honor it, and the whole room absorbs the result — a repeatable formula leaders can apply beyond formal offsites.
quotes: Researchers reviewing 21 studies involving more than 11,000 people found that a single interaction changes how willing people are to trust a completely different person.
One recent experience with someone trustworthy is enough to shift the baseline. In fact, after just one such interaction, people even overestimate how likely others are to prove trustworthy as well.
The reverse also holds true. After a betrayal, people become more suspicious of others who had nothing to do with it.
One person's broken promise can make everyone a little warier. One person's follow-through can make the whole team a little more willing to take a risk on one another.

Wise leaders use offsites, team meetings, and learning experiences to fill the team with demonstrations of trust. They don't do this for fun. They do it to create low-stakes situations where trust can be extended and rewarded.
The specific activity matters less than the structure and payoff: Team members extend trust, others honor it, and the whole room absorbs the result.
Good leaders don't wait for trust to develop on its own. They build the moments and experiences that produce it.
